children: By Heard on the Street Staff
This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day's most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you're not subscribed, sign up here.

Stocks rose. Renewed Middle East fighting and falling bond prices have weighed on stocks, but major indexes shrugged off those pressures on Wednesday after a rough start to the week. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq both ended about 0.5% higher, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 295 points, or 0.6%.

Oil stayed high. Brent crude futures have risen sharply in recent days, and didn't move much on Wednesday despite the stock-market recovery. Brent hovered above $95 a barrel as Iran and the U.S. traded attacks again, leaving any resolution to the long-simmering conflict distant.

Alphabet won a court victory, sending shares higher. A court ruled that the Google parent didn't have to break up its ad-tech business. The company was found to have illegally monopolized online advertising, but the judge in the case ordered changes in its behavior that stopped short of the Justice Department's request for a breakup. Its shares rose 0.5% on the day.

Uber cut 10% of its workforce. The ride-share company said in a letter to employees that it was downsizing to reduce management layers and reinvest in its future. The company had reported slower revenue growth and a soft outlook in its quarterly earnings report last month. Uber's stock rose 1.6%.
Oil companies are enjoying a profit boom driven by high prices for gas and diesel fuel. But that doesn't mean they are interested in building new refineries.

Owning and operating a refinery now is a lucrative business. Building a new one would involve billions of dollars and take years to develop. Oil executives don't believe the supply gap caused largely by the Iran war and Russia's invasion of Ukraine will last that long.

As a result, oil refiners are focusing on maximizing output now to take advantage of today's circumstances instead of contemplating an expansion. That approach puts them at odds with President Trump, who wants more refining to reduce prices at the pump.
Three Federal Reserve governors are set to speak at two events on Thursday ahead of the Fed's next interest-rate decision this month.
New U.S. trade-balance data from July are expected in the morning.
A reading of the U.S. services purchasing managers index is also due, offering a gauge of the services sector's growth in August.
